papers.title: The Systematic Parameter Optimization of Displacement Reactions for Tailored ZnS Nanostructure Morphologies
papers.abstract: Precise regulation of zinc sulfide (ZnS) nanostructure morphology remains a significant objective in semiconductor materials research, as functional performance is highly sensitive to variations in particle size and geometry. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of displacement reaction synthesis parameters to achieve controlled morphological engineering of ZnS nanostructures. The influence of precursor concentration, reaction temperature, pH, solvent characteristics, reaction time, and ionic strength on nucleation behavior and crystal growth dynamics was systematically examined. Through deliberate adjustment of these variables, diverse structural forms, including nanoparticles, nanorods, nanosheets, and hierarchical architectures, were consistently synthesized without relying on external templates or complex directing agents. The results demonstrate that supersaturation levels predominantly regulate nucleation rates, whereas temperature and pH significantly affect anisotropic growth and defect evolution. Additionally, solvent polarity and reaction duration contribute to surface energy stabilization and aggregation control, facilitating uniform crystallite size and structural homogeneity. Structural characterization verifies the formation of phase-pure, highly crystalline ZnS, while optical analysis reveals morphology-dependent shifts in band-gap energy attributable to quantum confinement and surface-state phenomena. Overall, the study delineates clear relationships between reaction conditions and resulting nanostructure morphology, providing a rational framework for scalable displacement-based synthesis of ZnS tailored for optoelectronic, photocatalytic, and sensing technologies.

papers.title: Fundamentals and Methodology for Magnetic-Core Integration
papers.abstract: Magnetic-Core (MC) integration is an effective approach to improving the efficiency and power density of power converters. Although numerous MC integration structures for inductors/transformers have been proposed, systematic MC integration methodologies, especially the design guidance for integrated core shape have rarely been studied over the years. Starting from the structure, function, and electromagnetic characteristics of magnetic components, the MCs are divided into two parts: 1) source-core, corresponding to the core surrounded by windings, 2) loop-core, corresponding to the core outside the windings. Based on the definition, it is revealed that the process of MC integration can be decomposed into two steps: 1) the realization of the coupling coefficient for source-cores, and 2) the sharing or integration design of the loop-cores. The above two steps can be unified as the regulation of flux in MCs. The regulation of source-core flux is to ensure that the coupling relationship between magnetic components before and after MC integration remains consistent with the requirements of the converter, while the regulation of loop-core magnetic flux aims to reduce the magnetic flux density, loss, and volume of the core. Based on the above theoretical foundation, the method to ensure the decoupling and regulation of coupling coefficients of sourcecores of multiple magnetic components, and the method for loopcore sharing or integration, and magnetic flux/magnetic density regulations are proposed for the MC integration design. Based on the proposed MC integration rules and methods, a CLLC resonant converter with integrated transformer/inductor is designed as an example. Feasibilities and effectiveness of the presented integrated MCs are verified with experimental results.

papers.title: Heatmap-Based Partial Discharge Screening Using an SDR+TEV Stack
papers.abstract: Can a low-cost software-defined radio (SDR) stack provide usable signatures for GIS-like partial discharge (PD) screening? This micro-study offers an initial confirmation using an SDRplay RSP1A receiver paired with a transient earth voltage (TEV) sensor and a heatmap-first post-processing workflow. A controlled protocol spans alternating PD/no-PD runs, fixed-gain (autogain-off) ablation, focused-frequency operation, and long-capture two-pass measurements. Evidence is intentionally lightweight: qualitative heatmap separability, supported by tail-sensitive spectral metrics on matched scenario pairs. Fixed-gain and long-capture conditions produce the most consistent PD-enhanced signatures, whereas autogain reduces separability in alternating wideband runs. Overall, the results suggest SDR+TEV monitoring can serve as a practical, IoT-oriented early-warning pipeline, and motivate further research on repeatability, calibration, and field deployment constraints.
